title: Cedarfield Financial - Dedicated capacity discovery
summary: Discovery focused on Cedarfield's need for reserved GPU capacity (Dedicated), network isolation, burst handling and scaling expectations. Key concerns: SOC2/compliance, KMS integration, predictable latency under peak trading hours, and cost tradeoffs between hosted vs dedicated. Next steps: size pilot cluster, share pricing and security pack, schedule performance benchmark with sample traces.
next_steps: Redwood to send Dedicated pricing + burst options (Ava)
Share security and SOC2 docs + network diagram (Diego)
Customer to provide 48h sample traffic traces and typical prompt sizes (Mark)
Schedule pilot kickoff + benchmark week (w/ Diego)
action_items: Ava Chen: Send Dedicated pricing deck and two sizing options (pilot + production) by 2026-11-20
Diego Ramos: Share SOC2, network diagram, and KMS integration guide by 2026-11-18
Mark Ellis: Upload 48h request traces and example prompts to shared folder by 2026-11-19
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-16
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Mark Ellis (Cedarfield, Head of ML), Priya Shah (CTO), Liam O'Connor (Infra Lead), Sara Kim (Product)

Summary (auto): discovery, focused on Dedicated reserved GPUs, isolation/VPC needs, and burst strategy for overnight batch & market open spikes.

[00:00] Ava Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm ava from redwood, i'll kick us off. quick round robin would be great, remind me who's on the line?
[00:08] Mark Ellis: hi ava, mark here, head of ml at cedarfield. we run a few inference workloads for customer support and trading ops.
[00:14] Priya Shah: priya, cto, i'll be listening for infra/security implications.
[00:18] Liam O'Connor: liam, infra, curious about network isolation and burst strategy.
[00:22] Sara Kim: sara from product, mostly focused on latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
[00:26] Diego Ramos: diego here, se on redwood, i'll do the technical deep dive part.

[00:35] Ava Chen: awesome. quick agenda - understand current stack, constraints, traffic patterns, then talk dedicated/reserved gpu options, burst behavior, and next steps. sound good?
[00:42] Priya Shah: yes, go ahead.

[01:05] Mark Ellis: to give context - we started with hosted apis for embeddings and summarization, but as volume grew and compliance needs tightened we need more isolation and predictable latency. around market open (9:30 ET) and end of day we see 3-5x spikes for inference. avg qps currently 60 during day and spikes to 300 for 15-20 minutes.

[01:40] Diego Ramos: ok that's helpful. are you currently using any caching or local prefix caching?
[01:45] Mark Ellis: minimal caching, mostly per-request generate. some teams built a small results cache but not prefix/KV level.

[02:05] Ava Chen: when you say isolation - are you looking for dedicated hardware in our environment or private deployment in your VPC/on-prem?
[02:13] Priya Shah: we prefer dedicated capacity in redwood's infra with VPC peering and customer-managed keys; we don't want model weights or logs commingled.
[02:22] Liam O'Connor: plus strict egress rules and audit logs, and ability to request forensics if needed.

[02:40] Diego Ramos: good - our Dedicated offering supports reserved GPU pools with VPC peering and KMS integration. we can do customer-managed keys, and audit logs forwarded to your SIEM. for burst handling we offer configurable burst capacity and autoscaling policies, but there are limits based on reservation sizes.

[03:12] Mark Ellis: can you give a sense of how burst works - like if we reserve 4 A100s but need 12 for 20 minutes, is that automatic?
[03:20] Diego Ramos: we have two patterns - warm reserved pool for baseline, and burst nodes that are either pre-warmed or pulled from a shared capacity (hosted spare) depending on contract. pre-warmed burst is faster but more expensive. shared spare can be provisioned but has slightly longer cold start and potential throttling during peak industry-wide demand.

[03:52] Priya Shah: what's the SLA on fallback? if shared spare not available, do we fail open to hosted, or queue?
[03:58] Diego Ramos: policy configurable - options are queue with priority, failover to a lower-capacity model variant, or route to hosted (if permitted by your data policy). many enterprise customers choose variant fallback plus queueing to maintain availability.

[04:25] Liam O'Connor: latency during spikes is critical - our SLAs require 95th pct under 250ms for short prompt len (<=256 tokens). can dedicated meet that with burst?
[04:33] Diego Ramos: yes for baseline reserved capacity we can provision to meet 95th pct <250ms; during burst it depends on whether burst nodes are pre-warmed. if you need strict latency SLOs during spikes, we recommend pre-warmed burst or slightly overprovision baseline.

[05:00] Mark Ellis: cost tradeoff then - how much more is pre-warmed burst vs shared spare?
[05:05] Ava Chen: rough ballpark - pre-warmed burst is 1.5-2x the baseline per-GPU cost for the reserved window because we're holding instances warm. shared spare is lower but billed on consumption and may have throttle windows. we'll share exact pricing in the deck.

[05:30] Priya Shah: compliance: SOC2, ISO, KMS, SSO (SAML), RBAC - can you walk through what's supported?
[05:38] Diego Ramos: we are SOC2 Type 2, support SAML/SSO for console, RBAC for roles, and KMS/HSM integrations for model keys and customer data encryption. audit logs can be exported to your logging endpoint. we'll send the security pack after this call.

[06:02] Sara Kim: for product - how do you handle model rollouts and version pinning?
[06:07] Diego Ramos: per-route model pinning, can do canary and A/B rollouts, automatic fallback policies, and tracing hooks for token-level cost/latency breakdowns. we also have per-model perf profiles to inform capacity sizing.

[06:28] Mark Ellis: great. about workload - prompts average 120 tokens, worst-case 2k tokens for some internal reports. batch jobs overnight generate a lot of long-context runs. how does long context change capacity?
[06:41] Diego Ramos: long contexts increase memory/KV cache pressure and reduce throughput; kernel selection and quantization matter. for mixed workloads we recommend separate pools for short-latency API and long-batch jobs or dedicated routes with different instance types.

[07:05] Priya Shah: separate pools means more reserved capacity overall - will you help model which workloads should be colocated?
[07:11] Ava Chen: yes we do workload profiling as part of onboarding; we can propose a split (e.g., 6 GPUs for low-latency real-time, 4 GPUs optimized for long-context batch).

[07:30] Mark Ellis: curious about KV/prefix caching - can we cache customer-specific prefixes?
[07:35] Diego Ramos: yes, prefix and KV caching supported. we can configure cache hot lanes for frequently used prefixes which dramatically reduce per-token cost and improve latency. but caching semantics have to be evaluated for privacy/PII.

[07:58] Liam O'Connor: about network - we need VPC peering and no public internet ingress for model artifacts. do you support complete egress control?
[08:08] Diego Ramos: we support VPC peering and customer-managed NAT/egress rules; model artifacts never cross public internet in Dedicated when configured with private deployment options. we can also enable private endpoint+JIT access.

[08:30] Priya Shah: what about data retention and logs? can we set retention windows and log scrubbers?
[08:37] Diego Ramos: yes retention is configurable and we can scrub logs for PII; audit logs forwarded to your SIEM, and raw model inputs can be disabled from retention.

[08:55] Mark Ellis: ok let me walk through our rough numbers - target steady state 6-8 GPUs for production low-latency (serving 60 qps avg), and overnight batch 4 GPUs for 8 hours. spikes up to +24 GPUs for 20 minutes at market open.

[09:18] Ava Chen: good, that gives us a baseline: production pool 8 GPUs, batch pool 4, burst pool up to 24 - so you'd want reserved baseline of 12 and burst to 24?
[09:27] Mark Ellis: maybe yes, but cost concern. can we do predictive autoscale where burst is allowed only if cost center approves?
[09:33] Diego Ramos: yes you can gate burst with approvals or set budget caps and automated rollback. We can also set scheduled scaling for predictable windows (market open) to reduce need for dynamic burst.

[09:55] Priya Shah: scheduled scaling sounds good - we'll schedule extra during market open. What's the provisioning lead time if we want pre-warmed nodes for market open?
[10:02] Diego Ramos: if pre-warmed we can schedule them; the contract defines the reservation window. For ad-hoc pre-warm, we recommend a 1-2 hour notice under typical operations, but we can support daily schedules as part of the reserved plan.

[10:28] Sara Kim: small question - do you expose token-level cost metrics per request?
[10:32] Diego Ramos: yes token-level cost/latency breakdowns and per-route billing are available in the console and via API.

[10:40] Mark Ellis: security again - KMS. we need CMEK where we control keys. is HSM available?
[10:46] Diego Ramos: we support CMEK via major cloud KMS providers; HSM-backed keys are supported for enterprise plans. We'll include the integration guide.

[11:02] Ava Chen: thinking about pilot - we usually propose a 4-week pilot with smaller reserved pool (e.g., 4 GPUs) and synthetic load tests + one real workload. does that align with your timeline?

[11:12] Mark Ellis: yes pilot makes sense. timeline: we'd like pilot by mid-december and production in q1 27. Need security review done before pilot.

[11:26] Priya Shah: security review timeline - we'll need SOC2 docs and network diagrams for our GRC team.

[11:32] Diego Ramos: we'll send the security package within 48 hours.

[11:40] Mark Ellis: one more technical - how do you handle model updates and version pinning during burst fallback? if a fallback model is different, we need to ensure quality.

[11:49] Diego Ramos: we support model variant pinning per route. fallback policies can route to lower-capacity variant of the same model family to preserve behaviour. We also surface eval metrics and regression alerts.

[12:09] Sara Kim: for our reports there's sometimes customer PII in prompts - can you guarantee input never stored?
[12:14] Diego Ramos: yes we can disable retention for those routes and ensure inputs aren't written to persistent storage; plus we can route logs only to your SIEM.

[12:28] Mark Ellis: ok sounds good. can you talk about monitoring and tracing? we need token-level traces and per-request latencies.

[12:36] Diego Ramos: we integrate with tracing systems and provide per-route dashboards; you can pull token-level traces for sampling. Also alerts for regressions tied to prompt-sets.

[12:54] Ava Chen: quick check - any blockers for you to proceed to pilot?
[12:59] Priya Shah: need security pack and clear pricing for scheduled pre-warm vs shared spare, and an option to cap burst costs.

[13:08] Mark Ellis: also need sample benchmark - can we run a performance test with our 48h traces?
[13:12] Diego Ramos: yes we'll run a benchmark in the pilot using your traces; please upload to shared folder.

[13:25] Liam O'Connor: about network egress - will you support private peering and no public ingress to the model endpoints? we need strict egress.
[13:33] Diego Ramos: yes, VPC peering and private endpoints available; we will work with your network team for allowed IP ranges and routing.

[13:48] Ava Chen: ok let's do a recap and owners. Ava will send pricing and two sizing options. Diego will send SOC2, KMS guide and network diagram. Mark will upload request traces and we'll schedule pilot for mid-december.

[14:03] Priya Shah: thanks. one last - competitors question: we're also evaluating an on-prem inference vendor and a managed cloud provider. cost and SLA will drive the decision.

[14:12] Ava Chen: understood. we'll include clear cost vs latency tradeoffs in the deck and include a sample TCO over 12 months.

[14:20] Mark Ellis: perfect. thanks everyone.

[14:24] Sara Kim: thanks.

[14:26] Diego Ramos: thanks all, we'll follow up.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker overlap and mishearing of acronyms (KMS/KMH), some proper nouns may be transcribed imperfectly.

End of call.
